questions.q: In Airflow's TaskFlow API, how do values typically move from one `@task` function to the next?
options: Through a shared global variable
Through Airflow's XCom mechanism, by returning and accepting values between task functions
Through a message queue the DAG author must configure manually
They cannot move between tasks at all
questions.explain: TaskFlow tasks pass values by returning them from one function and accepting them as an argument in the next; Airflow moves these under the hood using XComs.

questions.q: What is the key architectural difference between an Airflow TaskFlow task and a Kubeflow Pipelines `@dsl.component`?
options: There is no real difference; they are the same abstraction with different names
A TaskFlow task runs in the shared Airflow worker environment; a KFP component runs in its own independent container
KFP components cannot have inputs or outputs
TaskFlow tasks can only run on Kubernetes
questions.explain: Airflow TaskFlow tasks are Python functions executing inside a shared worker environment. KFP components are each independently containerized with their own base image.

questions.q: What does `compiler.Compiler().compile(...)` produce in a Kubeflow Pipelines v2 workflow?
options: A trained model file
A portable pipeline definition (IR YAML) that can run on any KFP-compatible backend
A Docker image pushed to a registry
A requirements.txt file
questions.explain: Compiling a `@dsl.pipeline` function produces a portable YAML/IR artifact describing the pipeline's DAG, which can run on Kubeflow Pipelines or compatible backends like Vertex AI Pipelines.

questions.q: In the KFP example, what does `Output[Model]` represent?
options: A plain Python return value with no tracking
A typed artifact that KFP wires to real artifact storage, readable by a downstream component's `Input[Model]`
A log message printed to stdout
A deprecated KFP v1 feature with no v2 equivalent
questions.explain: KFP typed artifacts like `Output[Model]`/`Input[Model]` are tracked, stored artifacts passed between independently containerized components — not just in-memory return values.

questions.q: Which scenario best explains why a team might choose Kubeflow Pipelines over Airflow for ML training steps?
options: They only run ordinary ETL jobs with no ML component
They need each training step to be bit-for-bit portable and reproducible across different environments, which the container boundary provides
They want to avoid writing any Python code
Airflow cannot run scheduled jobs
questions.explain: Kubeflow Pipelines' per-step containers make each step portable across environments, which is the main reason teams pick it over a shared-environment orchestrator like Airflow for training workloads.
